criteria.name: Institutional Mandate Alignment
criteria.description: Contribution to the central bank's statutory mandate, institutional objectives, and critical public capabilities.
anchors: No mandate relevance; placement change adds no institutional value
Limited relevance; administrative support only
Supports one institutional objective with moderate benefit
Strong contribution to several institutional objectives
Essential to the mandate or a systemically important capability

criteria.name: Capability Enablement and Strategic Flexibility
criteria.description: Extent to which the candidate architecture enables reusable capabilities, automation, interoperability, data services, and adaptable institutional delivery.
anchors: Candidate materially constrains required capabilities or future flexibility
Limited enablement with significant architectural constraints
Adequate enablement with identifiable trade-offs
Strong enablement across multiple reusable capabilities
Excellent enablement with strong strategic flexibility and governed reusable capabilities

criteria.name: Agility and Time to Capability
criteria.description: Ability of the candidate architecture and operating model to provide required capability within the needed timeframe without weakening governance.
anchors: Candidate cannot meet required time-to-capability
Slow delivery with substantial constraints
Acceptable delivery timeframe with manageable constraints
Strong delivery speed and adaptability
Excellent time-to-capability with governed reusable services

criteria.name: Service Criticality and Impact Tolerance
criteria.description: Institutional impact of loss, degradation, compromise, or delayed recovery. A high score means the candidate placement can meet the required controls.
anchors: Candidate cannot meet criticality and impact-tolerance requirements
Major gaps require exceptional controls
Requirements may be met with substantial conditions
Requirements can be met with standard enhanced controls
Candidate demonstrably meets critical-service requirements

criteria.name: Functional and Operational Complexity
criteria.description: Operational complexity of the candidate architecture, including procedures, support boundaries, dependencies, and end-to-end service behavior.
anchors: Operational complexity is unacceptable for the service
High complexity with substantial operating constraints
Moderate complexity with manageable operating requirements
Limited complexity with clear operating procedures and ownership
Standardized operating model with low complexity and clear service behavior

criteria.name: Demand Profile and Scalability
criteria.description: Fit between workload demand, capacity variability, and the elasticity characteristics of the candidate placement.
anchors: Demand profile is fundamentally incompatible
Limited fit and poor capacity economics
Mixed profile with conditional benefits
Strong fit for variable demand or planned scaling
Excellent fit with substantial elasticity or scheduling benefits

criteria.name: Service Dependencies and Integration
criteria.description: Dependency on identity, data, networks, security services, internal platforms, external providers, and other workloads.
anchors: Critical tightly coupled dependencies make the placement infeasible
Major dependencies require complex compensating architecture
Dependencies are manageable with documented tradeoffs
Mostly standards-based integrations with limited constraints
Loosely coupled, API- or event-driven dependencies with clear ownership

criteria.name: Architecture and Portability
criteria.description: Technical suitability, standards alignment, portability, substitutability, and ability to recover or relocate the workload without disproportionate redesign.
anchors: Highly proprietary or rigid architecture with no credible portability
Material provider-specific dependency and limited portability
Moderate portability with documented constraints
Portable architecture with viable alternatives
Highly portable, standards-based, automation-ready architecture with credible alternatives

criteria.name: Specialized Infrastructure and AI Requirements
criteria.description: Dependency on HSMs, accelerators, mainframes, specialized storage, dedicated networks, licensing devices, or embedded-AI capabilities.
anchors: Required infrastructure is unavailable or unacceptable
Available only through high-risk or highly constrained options
Available with significant architecture and operational conditions
Available through supported dedicated or managed capabilities
Fully supported with appropriate capacity, control, and lifecycle assurance

criteria.name: Connectivity, Latency, and Data Gravity
criteria.description: Network dependency, latency, throughput, data volume, synchronization, and proximity requirements.
anchors: Candidate cannot meet latency, throughput, or data-locality needs
Major connectivity or data-movement constraints
Requirements are achievable with material conditions
Requirements are achievable with engineered connectivity
Candidate provides strong performance, proximity, and connectivity assurance

criteria.name: Platform and Operational Readiness
criteria.description: Compatibility with target platforms, automation, observability and monitoring interfaces, support processes, skills, and lifecycle tooling.
anchors: No viable platform or operating capability for the candidate
Major platform, skills, interface, or tooling gaps
Candidate is viable subject to defined operating conditions
Strong platform compatibility and available operating capability
Mature standardized platform with automation, observability interfaces, and lifecycle controls

criteria.name: Lifecycle Cost Position
criteria.description: Expected lifecycle cost of the candidate architecture, including infrastructure or service consumption, software, support, facilities, personnel, resilience, security, and exit.
anchors: Lifecycle cost is disproportionate to the required service outcome
High lifecycle cost with limited compensating value
Lifecycle cost is broadly proportionate to requirements
Favorable lifecycle cost for the required service outcome
Strong lifecycle economics with transparent and sustainable cost drivers

criteria.name: Capacity and Utilization Efficiency
criteria.description: Ability of the candidate to provide required capacity, elasticity, performance, and utilization efficiency across the assessment horizon.
anchors: Capacity model is infeasible or materially inefficient
Significant capacity, utilization, or elasticity inefficiencies
Adequate capacity model with manageable inefficiencies
Strong capacity and utilization alignment
Excellent capacity efficiency, elasticity, and utilization transparency

criteria.name: Commercial and Licensing Flexibility
criteria.description: Licensing, subscription, contractual commitments, portability rights, and commercial flexibility associated with the candidate and its exit options.
anchors: Licensing or contract makes the placement economically infeasible
Material restrictions and likely duplicate cost
Feasible subject to negotiation and due diligence
Portable licensing or favorable subscription terms
Open, transferable, or fully substitutable commercial model

criteria.name: Comparative TCO and Exit Cost
criteria.description: Risk-adjusted lifecycle comparison including operation, connectivity, data transfer, resilience, support, reversibility, and exit costs.
anchors: Risk-adjusted TCO is materially unfavorable and exit is impracticable
Higher TCO with weak compensating benefits or material exit constraints
Comparable TCO; decision depends on nonfinancial requirements
Favorable TCO with credible exit provisions
Strong lifecycle economics and credible reversibility over the assessment horizon

criteria.name: Data Sensitivity and Security Controls
criteria.description: Fit with data classification, confidentiality, integrity, privacy, encryption, key custody, segmentation, privileged access, vulnerability management, and logging requirements.
anchors: Mandatory security requirements cannot be met
Major gaps require exceptional compensating controls
Requirements may be met with substantial conditions
Requirements can be met with approved enhanced controls
Candidate demonstrably satisfies all required security controls

criteria.name: Data and Control Sovereignty
criteria.description: Jurisdiction, residency, identity control, encryption-key ownership, administrative access, control-plane dependency, and support-location requirements.
anchors: Mandatory sovereignty requirements cannot be met
Material sovereignty exposure with limited institutional control
Conditional viability with contractual and technical safeguards
Strong institutional control with bounded external dependency
Full alignment with approved sovereignty and institutional-control requirements

criteria.name: Compliance and Auditability
criteria.description: Ability to satisfy applicable law, institutional policy, assurance, evidence, audit access, traceability, records management, and oversight obligations.
anchors: Mandatory compliance or audit rights cannot be met
Major assurance or evidence gaps
Requirements may be met through material conditions
Requirements can be met through approved standard controls
Candidate provides strong continuous evidence and auditability

criteria.name: Resilience, Recovery, and Provider Dependency
criteria.description: Availability, RTO, RPO, backup independence, cyber recovery, recovery testing, concentration, substitutability, reversibility, and exit feasibility.
anchors: Recovery or provider-dependency requirements cannot be met
Major resilience or exit gaps require exceptional measures
Requirements are achievable with material architecture conditions
Strong resilience with tested recovery and credible exit arrangements
Demonstrably resilient, recoverable, substitutable, and reversible

zones.name: On-Premises — Traditional Infrastructure
zones.responsibility: Institution responsible for infrastructure, operating system, middleware, solutions, and data.
zones.fit: Specialized, legacy, tightly coupled, latency-sensitive, or sovereignty-constrained workloads.
zones.constraints: Capacity elasticity, utilization efficiency, lifecycle planning, and institutional capability.

zones.name: On-Premises — Private Cloud
zones.responsibility: Institution retains the cloud platform and workload responsibility unless specific layers are outsourced.
zones.fit: Workloads requiring local control with standardized self-service, automation, and pooled infrastructure.
zones.constraints: Platform maturity, skills, lifecycle funding, control-plane resilience, and scale economics.

zones.name: On-Premises — CaaS
zones.responsibility: Institution controls local infrastructure; container-platform and workload responsibilities depend on the selected operating model.
zones.fit: Containerized workloads requiring local execution, data proximity, or institution-controlled infrastructure.
zones.constraints: Cluster lifecycle, supply-chain security, skills, resilience, and capacity management.

zones.name: Cloud — IaaS
zones.responsibility: Provider operates physical infrastructure and virtualization; the institution remains accountable for operating systems, solutions, access, configuration, and data unless these activities are sourced separately.
zones.fit: Workloads needing infrastructure-level control, portability, or specialized virtual infrastructure.
zones.constraints: Management-plane dependency, connectivity, licensing, configuration, variable cost, and exit.

zones.name: Cloud — CaaS
zones.responsibility: Provider responsibility depends on the CaaS offer; the institution remains accountable for workload configuration, solutions, identities, supply chain, and data.
zones.fit: Containerized workloads benefiting from managed control planes, elasticity, or rapid platform provisioning.
zones.constraints: Provider dependency, egress, jurisdiction, portability, supply chain, connectivity, and skills.

zones.name: Cloud — PaaS
zones.responsibility: Provider operates infrastructure, operating system, middleware, and runtime; the institution retains solution, configuration, identity, and data accountability.
zones.fit: Modern solutions using managed runtimes, databases, integration, analytics, or developer services.
zones.constraints: Service dependency, data portability, configuration limits, jurisdiction, and exit complexity.

zones.name: Cloud — SaaS
zones.responsibility: Provider operates the solution and underlying stack; the institution retains accountability for selection, configuration, access, integration, data governance, continuity, and exit.
zones.fit: Standardized capabilities where differentiation and infrastructure control are limited.
zones.constraints: Data control, audit rights, identity, integration, subcontractors, continuity, and exit.

zones.name: On-Premises — Specialized AI Infrastructure
zones.responsibility: Institution controls the infrastructure stack; model-platform and operational activities depend on the selected sourcing arrangement.
zones.fit: Sensitive inference, embedded-AI infrastructure, accelerators, or data-proximity requirements.
zones.constraints: Accelerator lifecycle, energy, model supply chain, skills, monitoring, and isolation.

zones.name: Cloud — Specialized AI Infrastructure
zones.responsibility: Provider supplies cloud AI infrastructure or platforms; institutional responsibility remains for approved use, models, data, identities, configuration, monitoring, and exit.
zones.fit: Elastic accelerator demand, experimentation, managed AI platforms, or burst capacity.
zones.constraints: Data exposure, model/provider dependency, jurisdiction, cost volatility, egress, and evidence.

zones.name: Hybrid — Composite Placement
zones.responsibility: Stack responsibility is determined separately for every on-premises and cloud component and integrated into one end-to-end accountability model.
zones.fit: Services deliberately distributed across local and cloud components for control, resilience, proximity, or capability.
zones.constraints: Operational complexity, synchronization, identity, observability, failure propagation, and accountability.

operations.name: None / Not applicable
operations.definition: No supplemental operating or support arrangement is recorded.

operations.name: Internal operation
operations.definition: Institution personnel perform the defined operational activities.

operations.name: Co-managed
operations.definition: Institution and provider divide activities through an explicit responsibility matrix.

operations.name: Outsourced / managed service
operations.definition: An external provider performs a broad, continuing operational scope under contracted service levels.

operations.name: Outtasked specialist service
operations.definition: A bounded specialist activity is externally performed without transferring end-to-end operation.
operations.use: Supplemental model; primary only where the assessed scope is itself the specialist service

operations.name: Provider-operated
operations.definition: The technology-service provider operates the stack layers inherent to the consumed service.

requirements.question: Were all materially relevant execution locations, service models, and external capabilities represented within one governed perimeter?
Were workload requirements characterized and multiple candidate arrangements assessed after mandatory gating rather than through a universal cloud/on-premises rule?
Are institutional decision rights, ownership, delegated execution, and assurance responsibilities explicitly recorded?
Are service dependencies, operational evidence, ITSM interfaces, security-monitoring interfaces, and recovery-status exchanges sufficiently defined?

requirements.principle: Security, sovereignty, and resilience by design
requirements.question: Does the candidate preserve required control over data, identity, keys, administration, jurisdiction, provider dependencies, reversibility, and exit?

requirements.principle: Security, sovereignty, and resilience by design
requirements.question: Are criticality, end-to-end recovery dependencies, disaster recovery, cyber/trusted recovery, and supporting evidence assessed?
Are lifecycle economics evaluated transparently without allowing lower cost to override mandatory institutional requirements?

Are AI infrastructure, embedded AI, and AI-enabled operations classified and governed according to data flows, dependencies, permissions, authority, oversight, auditability, suspension, and reversibility?
